dashboard.inboxExplainWhat: A holding area for links worth keeping before you know where they belong. Paste a URL onto the dashboard and it lands here, becomes a bookmark, or asks you which — whichever you chose under Behavior. The browser extension can save here too, and a URL already in the inbox is turned away rather than duplicated.
dashboard.inboxExplainRead: A new link stays unread until you open it. Keep (r) takes it out of the queue for good and puts it on the Kept tab, where it waits without a page until you file it. Read links stay in the list — being read is not a reason to remove something — and Clear read deletes them in one go when you are done with them. The tab badge counts only what is unread and awake.
dashboard.inboxExplainSnooze: Snoozing hides a link until a time you pick, so the list stays down to what you can act on now. Sleeping links are left out of every count and filter except Snoozed, and reappear on their own once the time passes.
dashboard.inboxExplainPromote: Promote turns a link into a real bookmark, opening the full form with the page and category left for you to choose. The inbox entry goes once the bookmark is saved, so nothing ends up filed in two places.
dashboard.inboxExplainTriage: Triage walks the list one link at a time without the mouse. Sorting oldest first is the other way through it: an inbox is cleared from the bottom, where the links you have been avoiding are. Filter, sort and search all appear in the address bar, so any view can be bookmarked or shared.

dashboard.analyticsNoticeBody: Analytics is off. Turning it on shares anonymous usage statistics so it is visible which features are used and what can be improved — never bookmark names, URLs, or searches. You can switch it back off at any time.
dashboard.analyticsNoticeWhyBody: nextDash had no picture of how it is actually used. Which views do people open? Does anyone use finders, the tag cloud, or the inbox? Where do people give up halfway through adding a bookmark? Without answers, every improvement is guesswork. These statistics answer exactly that — which features get used and what can be made better — and nothing else. They are not meant to follow you around: it is purely abstract, technical measurement of flow and feature usage, aggregated across everyone. Turning it on helps a lot, even if you only leave it on for a few days — a short stretch of real usage already says more than months of guessing, and you are welcome to switch it back off afterwards.
dashboard.analyticsNoticeNeverBody: No bookmark names, URLs, search queries, page or category names, notes, or tags. No cookies are set, no personal profile is built, and you are not tracked across other websites. Counts that could be revealing are rounded into buckets, and the instance is self-hosted, so nothing is shared with an advertising network.
dashboard.analyticsNoticeOnBody: Go to Config → Behavior → Privacy & sync and tick "Privacy-friendly analytics", or run :telemetry on from the command palette. It applies after the page reloads. While it is off, the tracker is not loaded at all and no request leaves your machine.

dashboard.changesTourCardTitleNew: A minute on where things are
dashboard.changesTourCardBody: A short tour of what stands somewhere else now — about a minute, and you can put the old arrangement back as you go.
dashboard.changesTourCardBodyNew: A short tour of the header, the buttons and config — about a minute.
dashboard.changesTourPagesTitleNew: Your pages live in the header
dashboard.changesTourPagesBody: The tabs still stand beside Inbox, Health and Config. New is that three other styles put them in the middle of the header. The page you were last on stays marked, also while you are in Config.
dashboard.changesTourPagesBodyNew: Every page has a number key, and the tabs stand beside Inbox, Health and Config. Three other styles put them in the middle of the header instead.
dashboard.changesTourActionsTitle: The action buttons have a place of their own
dashboard.changesTourActionsTitleNew: The action buttons stand at an edge
dashboard.changesTourActionsBody: They stand in a column on the right, which slides into the edge after a couple of seconds. Touching that edge, clicking the handle it leaves behind, or pressing ' or Shift + O brings them back. Their key chips can go; the keys keep working.
dashboard.changesTourConfigBody: Appearance and Behavior show their settings straight away, in tabs, with a live preview beside Appearance. Date & weather sits under Appearance, and there is a Logs section.
dashboard.changesTourWorkbenchBody: Filters on the left, the list in the middle, an edit panel on the right — for several bookmarks at once as well as one.
dashboard.changesTourWidgetsBody: A Custom widget reads your own JSON address and puts the numbers on the dashboard as figures, rows or a bar. You say which field goes where and how often it refreshes.
dashboard.changesTourTagsBody: Saving a bookmark offers tags from the page itself and from the tags you already use. Clicking one takes it; you only type what is not there.
dashboard.changesTourLooksBody: Gloss themes catch the light and carry a badge in the theme browser, and a theme of your own can set its shape and its sheen, in a light and a dark half. Shift + A opens the browser from anywhere.
dashboard.changesTourDoneBody: You can open this again from Config → Help → Guided tours, or with the :changes command. The full release notes are in What's new.
dashboard.clockWeatherBody: Name a town and the header shows its weather beside the date. The clock and the unit are yours to pick too.
dashboard.clockWeatherSaveFailed: Could not save. The same settings are in Config → Appearance → Date & weather.
dashboard.freshNoticeTitle: Some of these pages have moved on
dashboard.feedQuietMark: Publishes a feed — nothing new since you last opened this
dashboard.freshNoticeBody: A blog, a changelog, a status page — nextDash can put a small count on the ones that have published something since you last opened them, and gather them in a Fresh collection. No articles are stored; it is a count, not a reader.
dashboard.freshTutorialEnabled: Fresh is on. Counts appear as the feeds are read.
dashboard.freshTutorialStep1Title: A count on the rows that moved
dashboard.freshTutorialStep1Body1: Some of the pages you save keep publishing: a blog, a changelog, a forum, a status page. You cannot tell by looking at the row, so you either open them on the off-chance or stop opening them at all.
dashboard.freshTutorialStep1Body2: With Fresh on, a bookmark whose page has published something since you last opened it carries a small count. Opening it clears the count. That is the whole of what you have to do.
dashboard.freshTutorialStep2Title: And a collection that gathers them
dashboard.freshTutorialStep2Body1: The same bookmarks gather in a Fresh collection between your categories, newest publication first, with the number in its title. It appears only when something is actually new — an empty Fresh would be a section that means nothing.
dashboard.freshTutorialStep2Body2: It behaves like any other collection: it can be collapsed, and the rows in it are the real bookmarks, so editing one there edits it everywhere.
dashboard.freshTutorialStep3Body1: Switching Fresh on looks for feeds: it reads the head of each page you have saved, notes any feed advertised there, and remembers the pages that have none so it does not ask them again for a month. That is one request per bookmark, once.
dashboard.freshTutorialStep3Body2: Known feeds are then asked once an hour, and each request only asks whether anything changed — a quiet site answers “no” in a few hundred bytes. A feed that keeps failing is retired rather than retried forever.
dashboard.freshTutorialNotReader: Most saved pages carry no feed at all. Config → Behavior → Inbox & Fresh says how many of yours do.
dashboard.freshTutorialStep4Body1: An empty dashboard is the usual answer, and it is not a fault: a shop, a wiki page, a login screen publishes nothing. The Inbox & Fresh tab counts it out for you — “12 of 40 bookmarks asked · 2 publish a feed” — with Find feeds now to look again after you have saved something new.
dashboard.freshTutorialStep4Body2: And Fresh is not a feed reader: no articles, no headlines, no read state of its own — only how many entries are newer than your last visit. The switch is under Config → Behavior → Inbox & Fresh, on the tab it shares with the inbox.
dashboard.spreadTutorialStep1Body1: A category normally lives in one column and grows downwards. A long one therefore towers over its neighbours, and the bookmarks past the limit disappear behind "+ N more".
dashboard.spreadTutorialStep1Body2: Let it spread and the same bookmarks flow across two or three columns instead — same height as everything around it, more of it visible at once. It suits the categories made of many short entries.
dashboard.spreadTutorialStep2Title: Switch it on where the category is
dashboard.spreadTutorialStep2Body1: Right-click a category header and pick Spread across columns, or press Shift+W with the category focused. It applies straight away — no reload, no settings page.
dashboard.spreadTutorialStep2Body2: The same entry reads "Back to one column" once it is on, so the way out is where the way in was. Every category decides for itself; its neighbours are untouched.
dashboard.spreadTutorialStep3Title: You do not pick the number of columns
dashboard.spreadTutorialStep3Body1: How wide a spread category gets follows from two things you have already set: Items per category, which caps the height of one column, and how many bookmarks are in it. Forty bookmarks at fifteen per column need three.
dashboard.spreadTutorialStep3Body2: So it grows when you add bookmarks and shrinks when you delete them, and it never takes more columns than the grid has. That also means Items per category cannot be Unlimited while anything spreads — with no column height, nothing decides how many columns are needed.
dashboard.spreadTutorialStep4Body1: Config → Structure → Categories has the same switch as a ↔ button on every row, which is the quicker way to go through a page in one sitting.
dashboard.spreadTutorialStep4Body2: Under Appearance → Grid you will find what applies to all of them: whether a new category starts out spread, and a button that switches spreading off again — for this page or for every page.
dashboard.categorySpreadUnavailable: There is only one column to work with — spreading needs at least two.
dashboard.categorySpreadNeedsLimit: Spreading needs a limit on items per category — that limit is what decides how many columns a category takes. Set one in Config → Appearance → Grid.

dashboard.healthHeaderTitleHint: This view lists bookmarks that need attention: broken links, content that no longer matches what was expected, and monitors that are down. The path above shows the active filter.
dashboard.healthTrendHelpWhat: The share of your bookmarks that counted as healthy on each day, going back {days} days.
dashboard.healthTrendHelpAxis: The axis is fixed at 0–100%, so the line only moves when the number really moves. A collection sitting between 91% and 93% looks flat here, which is the honest picture — scaling to the range would turn that into a cliff.
dashboard.healthTrendHelpGaps: A reading is recorded when the health report runs, so days you did not open nextDash leave a gap and the line breaks rather than guessing across it.
dashboard.healthTrendHelpHealthy: Healthy means reachable if checking is on, opened recently enough, and not clashing with another bookmark — the same rule the Healthy tile counts.
dashboard.healthSettingsLinkHint: Check interval, alert threshold, maintenance windows and downtime alerts
dashboard.healthTrendChartLabel: Healthy bookmarks over the last {days} days, from {first}% to {last}%
dashboard.healthFleetCollapse: Hide least-available monitors and outages, keep just the uptime tiles
dashboard.healthExplainScore: Every bookmark starts at 100 and loses points for each thing wrong with it — unreachable, never opened, a duplicate address, a clashing shortcut. Click the badge on a row, or press s, to see exactly what it was charged for.
dashboard.healthExplainTiles: A bookmark can be several things at once, so one that is both a duplicate and never opened is counted by both tiles and appears under either filter. The row itself shows only its worst problem, which is what decides its colour and its place in the list.
dashboard.healthExplainFresh: The report is built on the server and cached for a few minutes, so the header says how old it is. Retest all rebuilds it and re-tests everything that opted in to checking.
dashboard.healthExplainUptime: Only monitored bookmarks keep history. A percentage is followed by the number of checks behind it, because 100% from three checks is a much weaker claim than 100% from three hundred. A window with no checks at all reads "no data" rather than 0%.
dashboard.healthExplainFleet: On the Monitored filter, the panel above the list pools every monitor. Its uptime counts individual checks rather than averaging each monitor's percentage, so a monitor with three recorded checks cannot outweigh one with three thousand.
dashboard.healthExplainTrend: One point is recorded per day that you open this view, kept for 90 days. The line is drawn on a fixed 0–100 scale so a collection sitting between 91% and 93% looks as flat as it is, and days you did not visit leave a gap rather than a straight line through them.
dashboard.healthNoteBroken: These did not respond when they were last checked. Re-check one to test it again now, or open it to see for yourself.
dashboard.healthNoteDuplicate: Two or more bookmarks point at the same address. Merging keeps one row and folds the other's tags and notes into it.
dashboard.healthNoteUnchecked: Checking is switched on for these, but no check has run recently — so their status is unknown rather than bad.
dashboard.healthNoteMonitored: These are checked by the server on their own interval, which is what builds the uptime history and the panel below.
dashboard.healthNoteStale: You have opened these before, but not in the last 30 days. Nothing is wrong with them — they are candidates for tidying up.
dashboard.healthNoteUnused: These have never been opened since they were added. Often worth keeping, sometimes worth deleting, but always worth a look.
dashboard.healthNoteShortcutConflict: More than one bookmark claims the same keyboard shortcut, so pressing it is a coin toss between them.
dashboard.healthNoteOrphanedCategory: These point at a category that no longer exists on their page, usually because it was deleted without moving them first. They still work, but on the dashboard they sit with the uncategorized ones — edit a row to file it somewhere that exists.
dashboard.healthNoteMissingPreview: No title, description or image has been fetched yet, so these rows have little to show beyond their address.
dashboard.healthNoteCertificates: These sit on a host whose TLS certificate expires soon. The count above is hosts; this list is the bookmarks on them.
dashboard.healthNoteHealthy: Nothing is wrong with these: reachable if they are checked, opened recently enough, and not clashing with anything.

dashboard.healthTutorialStep1Title: Health can do more than "is it up?"
dashboard.healthTutorialStep1Body1: A few checks in this release: watching for a page that quietly changed underneath a link, expected downtime that should not page anyone, and alerts that land in Slack, Discord, Telegram, Pushover or ntfy instead of a raw webhook nobody reads.
dashboard.healthTutorialStep1Body2: This walks through all of it on one example — a status page you host yourself. Six short steps, then you are done. Config → Help → Health has the same walkthrough if you want it again later.
dashboard.healthTutorialStep2Body1: Right-click a bookmark, or open its editor, and set availability checking to Monitor instead of Periodic. This is your own server — worth checking on a schedule whether or not the dashboard happens to be open.
dashboard.healthTutorialStep2Body2: A Check interval row appears once it is monitored. A status page people rely on deserves closer watching than a personal blog — 5 minutes is a reasonable start.
dashboard.healthTutorialStep3VisualHint: Status codes that count as healthy
dashboard.healthTutorialStep3Body1: The status page sits behind a login, so it always answers 401 when the check has no session — normal, not a failure. Typing 200,401 into Status codes that count as healthy keeps a real outage from getting lost in the noise of an expected 401.
dashboard.healthTutorialStep3Body2: If the page also shows a phrase only when the service it reports on is actually healthy — "All systems operational", say — Text the page must contain catches a page that loads fine but is quietly reporting its own incident.
dashboard.healthTutorialStep4Title: Watch for the page changing shape entirely
dashboard.healthTutorialStep4Body1: Watch for redirects, retitling and rewrites keeps a baseline of where the link goes, what the page is titled, and roughly what it says — set once the checkbox is ticked, on the next check.
dashboard.healthTutorialStep4Body2: A domain that lapses or a proxy that quietly starts sending traffic elsewhere would sail straight past the status-code and keyword rules above, because the request never reaches the real page at all. This is the check that still notices.
dashboard.healthTutorialStep5Title: Tell it about the backup window
dashboard.healthTutorialStep5Body1: The service restarts nightly at 3am for its backup. Without a maintenance window, that alone raises an incident and an alert every single night — and after a week of that, a real 3am outage reads exactly like the six before it that meant nothing.
dashboard.healthTutorialStep5Body2: Config → Behavior → Status & alerts → Maintenance windows takes a day, a start time and an end time. Checks still run and the heartbeat still records what happened — only the alerting is held back.
dashboard.healthTutorialStep6Title: Get told when it actually breaks
dashboard.healthTutorialStep6Body1: Downtime alerts now has a Service picker, so the message actually lands somewhere readable instead of a block of raw JSON a chat app silently drops. Pick the one your team already watches — only the fields that service needs are shown.
dashboard.healthTutorialStep6Body2: Set Alert after to 3 so one dropped check during a blip does not page anyone, and click Send test alert once before trusting it with the real thing — a wrong chat ID otherwise fails silently, with nothing on screen to say why.
dashboard.healthTutorialStep6Closing: That is the whole loop: a heartbeat bar, an uptime percentage, and a message where you will actually see it — only when something is truly wrong.
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep1Title: A place for links you have not decided about yet
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep1Body1: Not every link worth keeping has a page and a category waiting for it. Paste a URL onto the dashboard and — depending on Paste destination under Config → Behavior — it lands here, becomes a bookmark straight away, or asks you which. The browser extension can save here too, and a URL already waiting is turned away rather than saved twice.
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep1Body2: Nothing in here is a bookmark yet, and nothing expires. Leaving a link sitting for a week costs nothing — that is what the list is for. Seven short steps and you will know every way back out of it.
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep2Title: Read is not the same as dealt with
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep2VisualHint: Clear read empties them in one go
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep2Body1: A new link stays unread until you open it or press r. Opening marks it read; r marks it read without opening, which is the quick way to say "yes, I still want this" about a link you already recognise.
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep2Body2: Read links stay in the list. Having read something is not a reason to throw it away, so removing them is a separate, deliberate act — Clear read in the toolbar deletes them all at once. The number on the Inbox tab counts only what is unread and awake, so nothing that is read or snoozed keeps nagging at you.
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep3Title: Snooze the ones that are not for today
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep3Body1: z hides a link until a time you pick — in 3 hours, tomorrow, this weekend, next week, or a date of your own. While it sleeps it is left out of every filter and every count except Snoozed, and it comes back on its own when the time is up. Wake now brings one back early.
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep3Body2: This is the habit that keeps the list honest. An inbox full of things you cannot act on right now is an inbox you stop reading — so if a link is genuinely for next month, snooze it to next month instead of scrolling past it thirty times first.
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep4Title: Write down why you saved it
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep4VisualNote: for the rate-limit section — compare with the other proposal
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep4Body1: n leaves a note on a link. Two weeks later the title alone rarely says why it mattered, and a link you can no longer explain to yourself is one you end up deleting unread. One line is enough.
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep4Body2: The Noted filter collects everything you have annotated, so a half-finished piece of research can be picked back up as a set rather than hunted for row by row. The note travels with the link into the bookmark form when you promote it, so the reason is not lost at the moment it becomes permanent.
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep5Title: Promote turns a link into a real bookmark
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep5VisualHint: Opens the full bookmark form, page and category still yours to pick
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep5Body1: p opens the bookmark form with the URL, title and note already filled in, leaving you the one decision the inbox deliberately postponed: which page and which category. Tags, icon, description and health checking are all there too, the same as any other new bookmark.
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep5Body2: Once the bookmark is saved the inbox entry goes, so nothing ends up filed in two places. If you would rather keep a record of everything that passed through, turn off Delete after promote under Behavior and promoted links stay behind, marked read. Cancelling the form changes nothing — the link is still sitting where it was.
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep6Title: Triage: the whole backlog, no mouse
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep6Body1: Deciding about forty links one row at a time is slow mostly because of everything else on screen. t puts a single link in front of you with nothing around it: j and k move, o or Enter opens, r keeps, z snoozes, n notes, p promotes, d deletes, Escape leaves. Each decision is one keystroke and the next link is already there.
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep6Body2: Set the sort to oldest first before you start. An inbox is cleared from the bottom, where the links you have been avoiding for a month are; the top is the part that still looks interesting and never actually needs you.
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep7Title: Selecting, narrowing, and sharing the view
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep7Body1: x ticks a row, Shift with the arrow keys extends the selection, Ctrl/Cmd+A takes everything currently listed — and the toolbar actions then apply to the lot. Bulk promote is the exception worth knowing: it asks once which page the links belong on and files them all there, instead of opening the form forty times.
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep7Body2: The Site dropdown narrows the list to one domain, which is how you find out that a single newsletter has quietly filled a third of your inbox. Filter, sort, search and site all show up in the address bar, so any view of the inbox can be bookmarked or sent to yourself on another machine.
dashboard.inboxTutorialStep7Closing: That is the whole loop: links land in one place, and leave it as a bookmark, a snooze, or a deletion — never by being quietly forgotten.

dashboard.widgetsTutorialStep1Title: A block that answers “what is going on”
dashboard.widgetsTutorialStep1Body1: A dashboard of links answers “where do I go”. A widget answers the other question: how much is waiting, what is down, how full the disk is. It sits among your categories, is dragged into place like one, and is one or two columns wide.
dashboard.widgetsTutorialStep1Body2: Most of them need nothing set up at all. And one of them — the custom widget — points at any address on your network that answers with JSON, which is what puts the services you run on the page beside the links to them. Six short steps.
dashboard.widgetsTutorialStep2Title: Thirteen tiles that read what nextDash already keeps
dashboard.widgetsTutorialStep2Body1: Health, Uptime, Certificates and Trend report what the health view reports. Inbox says what is waiting, Feeds which feed went quiet, Sources which import failed. Neglected, Blind spots, Duplicates, Archive, Trash and Backups each name a kind of tidying.
dashboard.widgetsTutorialStep2Body2: None of them polls anything new: the figures are already on disk and had nowhere to show. Click a figure and you land on the rows behind it, filtered.
dashboard.widgetsTutorialStep3Title: Each one has a few settings, and no more
dashboard.widgetsTutorialStep3Body1: What it counts, how many rows it shows, what it is called, how wide it is. Leave the title empty and the tile uses its type’s name. A tile that leaves rows out says how many, because five of twelve should not look like five of five.
dashboard.widgetsTutorialStep3Body2: Shown takes a widget off the dashboard without deleting it or losing its settings — the same switch the Close entry on the dashboard writes.
dashboard.widgetsTutorialStep4Title: The custom widget: any address that answers JSON
dashboard.widgetsTutorialStep4Body1: Give it an address, then name the fields you want by their path into the answer — totalRecords, cpu.load, data.0.name. Each becomes a figure on the tile, with a label you choose and a shape: a count, a percentage, bytes, a duration, a date, or plain text.
dashboard.widgetsTutorialStep4Body2: A path into a list works too, so an endpoint that returns items can be drawn as rows rather than figures. Nothing is hard-coded per service: if it speaks JSON over HTTP, it can be a tile.
dashboard.widgetsTutorialStep5Body1: Pick a preset and the address shape, the fields and the labels arrive already written — media servers and downloaders, the network boxes, the machine itself, and the everyday apps. You edit it from there rather than starting at a blank form.
dashboard.widgetsTutorialStep5Body2: A preset is a starting point, not a lock: change a path, drop a figure, point it at a different host. And a service nobody has written down yet is the same form with the fields left blank.
dashboard.widgetsTutorialStep6Title: The request is made by the server, and the key stays there
dashboard.widgetsTutorialAuthHint: Kept on the machine running nextDash, out of the page and out of your backups
dashboard.widgetsTutorialStep6Body1: The tile’s address is fetched by nextDash itself, not by your browser. That is what lets a widget read a service your browser cannot reach at all, and it keeps the token out of a page anyone can view the source of.
dashboard.widgetsTutorialStep6Body2: It inherits the same protections as every other outbound request — the address checks and the rate limit — and a widget that needs a sign-in says so on the tile rather than failing quietly.
dashboard.widgetsTutorialStep7Title: On the page it behaves like a category
dashboard.widgetsTutorialStep7Body1: Drag the // in its title to move it among your categories, click the header to fold it away, and right-click it for rename, width, settings and close. The arrow keys walk into a tile and through its rows, and Enter on a row does what clicking it does.

Between 30 seconds and 24 hours. Leaving it empty gives 5 minutes.

Choose it by what you are measuring: 30 to 60 seconds for a download speed or processor load, 5 minutes for a queue or a count, an hour for something that is only measured hourly. Asking more often than the service itself measures returns the same answer.

config.helpFreshBody:
Fresh tells you whether a site you bookmarked has published something since you last opened it — a blog, a changelog, a forum thread, a status page.

What you see. A bookmark with something new carries a small count on its row. The same bookmarks gather in a Fresh collection, newest first. Opening the bookmark clears its count.

Where the feed comes from. Switching Fresh on (Behavior → Inbox & Fresh) reads the head of each saved page once and notes any RSS or Atom feed it advertises. Pages without one are not asked again for a month. Find feeds now repeats the round and says how many bookmarks publish a feed.

Which bookmarks take part. The bookmark editor shows a Feed line when there is one. status:feed lists them in search, -status:feed the rest. Mark rows that publish puts a quiet dot on those rows even when nothing is new; it is off by default.

What it costs. Feeds are polled on the background re-check interval with a conditional request, so a quiet site answers with a few bytes. A feed that fails five times in a row is dropped.

What it is not. Not a feed reader: no articles are stored, only how many entries are newer than your last visit. Fresh is off until you turn it on, because it makes requests to other people's servers. For headlines on the dashboard, use the RSS widget.
config.feedsNote: A bookmark whose page advertises a feed can say how much it has published since you last opened it — a small count on the row, and a Fresh collection. Switching it on looks for feeds on the pages you have saved, then asks each one it found, hourly, with a conditional request a quiet site answers in a few hundred bytes. Off by default, because it is the one feature here that talks to other people's servers on your behalf. Most pages carry no feed: the line below says how many of yours do.

config.feedsInfoMessage: Bookmarks whose page advertises an RSS or Atom feed get a small count of what has been published since you last opened them, and appear in a Fresh collection. • Type a finder shortcut (e.g., "YT") and press space to automatically switch to finder mode.
• If a bookmark has the same shortcut as a finder, both options will appear for selection.
config.shortcutOpenModeEnterBody: Typing only filters the list. The shortcut you typed leads it, and Enter opens it. Nothing can decide for you that you had finished typing.
config.shortcutOpenModeDelayBody: The shortcut opens on its own once you stop typing for a moment. Keep typing and it stays out of the way.
config.shortcutOpenModeInstantBody: No Enter, no pause — the fastest, and the one that can swallow an ordinary word that starts with the same letters.
config.shortcutOpenModeInfoMessage:
The dashboard is always listening: what you type goes to the search line whether or not the panel is open. This decides when a bookmark shortcut acts on that.

• Press Enter to open — typing only narrows the list, and the shortcut you typed leads it. One keystroke more, and the same behaviour every day.
• Open after a short pause — the shortcut opens by itself once you stop typing for about half a second. Fast, and a word that carries on past the shortcut keeps going. A word typed slowly can still fall through the pause.
• Open the moment it matches — what nextDash did before v1.2.0. It costs no keystroke at all, and it can swallow an ordinary word that begins with the same letters: on an install with 200 shortcuts, eight of thirteen everyday search words were cut off mid-word — "invoice" opened something at "in" and left "voice" behind.

Open the moment it matches is the default again. Making Enter the default in v1.2.0 was a mistake: it treated a rare collision as the normal case, and charged every shortcut a second keystroke to prevent it. If a word of yours does get swallowed, the other two modes are here, and a shortcut that clashes can be renamed.
config.detectSoftNotFoundLabel: Spot pages that answer 200 but say "not found"
config.detectSoftNotFoundInfoTitle: Pages that are gone without saying so
config.detectSoftNotFoundInfoMessage:
The most common form of link rot is not a dead server. It is a page that answers perfectly and shows "page not found" — a CMS serving its error template with a success code, a docs site that swallowed a moved article, a shop whose product is no longer listed. Every ordinary check calls that healthy, because at the network level it is.

With this on, a monitored bookmark's check reads the page and judges the title first, then the opening of the body. A hit is recorded as a failure with the reason "Page says it does not exist", so it shows on the row, in the outage list and in the export like any other.

The cost is one bounded body read per monitored check, which is why it is a choice. An explicit expectation still wins: if you have said what the page must contain, that is what decides.

For the pages that never say so in words, the check also asks the host itself: one request to an address on that site which cannot exist, once per site per day. If that answers 200 too, a 200 from this host proves nothing, and a page matching that answer in length is taken to be it. A site that sends every address to a sign-in page is left alone — a gated app answers the probe and your bookmark with the same login screen, which looks identical and is not the same thing. What separates them is that a not-found page answers where it was asked, and a gate sends you somewhere else.
config.showGridKeyLegendInfoTitle: The key legend under the grid
config.showGridKeyLegendInfoMessage:
A short row of keys under the bookmarks, for the moves that are not obvious: arrows to select, j and k to move on, Enter to open, Escape to let go.

It stays out of the way until you start moving with the keyboard, appearing after the first keystroke and going again as soon as you open something — so it teaches while you are learning and disappears once you are not.
config.keepSearchOpenWhenEmptyInfoMessage:
When enabled, the search UI stays open even with an empty query.

• Good for keyboard-only workflows
• Can feel busier if you prefer a minimal idle state
config.showTagCloudButtonInfoMessage: Shows a / button stacked with What's new (desktop). Press / or click to open a tag word cloud (larger = more used). Click or Enter/Space toggles tags in the filter — the modal stays open so you can combine several. Bookmarks match any selected tag (OR). Active tags appear as chips under the title (each with ×) and on the / FAB (#work +1 when multiple). Arrow keys move between tags and Clear tag filter. Escape in the cloud closes the modal; Escape on the dashboard clears all filters. Clear tag filter removes every tag. • Related: :tag work in command mode lists bookmarks in the palette without changing the dashboard • Desktop / wide layout only — hidden on mobile • On by default (desktop only) • Turn off here to hide the button and modal entirely
config.maxPageTabsInfoMessage: How many pages the header draws before the rest are folded onto the +N chip. Between 3 and 9; the page you are on is always one of them, and `,` opens the panel with every page in it whatever this is set to.
config.maxHeaderActionsInfoMessage: How many action buttons stand in the header before the rest fold behind one control. Their keys keep working either way, and a button you switched off is in neither place.
config.pageSwitcherStyleInfoMessage: How the pages are drawn in the header. Numbers beside the destinations puts them at the right, next to inbox, health and config, and underlines the page you are on. One segmented control keeps a target per page inside a single box in the middle. Plain text drops the box and underlines the page you are on, in the middle. One button names the page you are on and opens the panel for the rest.
config.showPagesButtonInfoMessage: The action that opens the page panel, beside search and recents. Hiding it leaves `,` working — the panel is the same one, and the header simply stops drawing a way to it.
config.showInboxButtonInfoMessage: The inbox tab in the destinations, on the right of the header. Shift+I opens the inbox whether or not the button is drawn.
config.showDashboardButtonInfoMessage: The way back: it returns to the page of bookmarks you left, without a reload, and is lit while the dashboard is what you are looking at. The page tabs and the digits 1-9 go to the same place.
config.showConfigButtonInfoMessage: The gear on the right of the header. Shift+S opens config whether or not the button is drawn.
config.showAddBookmarkButtonInfoMessage: The + at the left of the action group, which opens the form for a new bookmark. `+` does the same from the keyboard whether or not the button is drawn.
config.showSearchButtonInfoMessage: Opens the search panel, which is also where commands and finders live — `>` opens it, and `:` and `?` open it in those two modes.
config.showCommandsButtonInfoMessage: A second door into the search panel, opened in command mode. `:` does the same, which is why this ships off: one panel with three modes needs one way in, not three.
config.showFindersButtonInfoMessage: A third door into the search panel, opened in finder mode. `?` does the same, so this ships off for the same reason the commands button does.
config.showRecentButtonInfoMessage: Opens the panel of bookmarks you opened last. `*` does the same from the keyboard whether or not the button is drawn.
config.showCollapseAllButtonInfoMessage: Folds every category on the page at once, and unfolds them again. `.` does the same, so this ships off — it is a key you press rarely and a button you pass constantly.
config.showCheatSheetButtonInfoMessage: Opens the list of every key the dashboard answers to. `!` does the same, and this is the button that teaches the others, so it ships on.
config.showPageTabsInfoMessage:
Controls whether page navigation tabs are visible.

• On: click/tap tabs to switch pages
• Off: switch pages using keyboard shortcuts only
config.showPageNamesInTabsInfoMessage:
Controls tab labels when tabs are visible.

• On: show page names
• Off: show page numbers
config.hideEmptyCategoriesInfoMessage:
When enabled, categories with no bookmarks are hidden on the dashboard.

• Keeps the dashboard tidy
• Empty categories are still visible in config → categories
config.alwaysCollapseCategoriesInfoMessage:
When enabled, categories start collapsed when dashboard data loads.

• Cleaner first view
• Requires extra clicks to open content each session
config.duplicateElsewhere: You already saved this link somewhere else.
config.deleteAllBookmarksHint: Removes every bookmark on every page. Your pages, categories, and all settings stay exactly as they are — and no default sample bookmarks are added back. This cannot be undone.
config.pwaInstallHint: Install nextDash for launcher-style access (pairs well with HyprMode).
config.checkModePeriodicHint: Checks once a day and flags the bookmark when it breaks.
config.checkModeMonitorHint: Checks on your own interval and keeps uptime history, a heartbeat and outage alerts. Includes everything Periodic does.
config.checkModeExplainPeriodic: Answers one question: is this link still alive? It is checked in the background about once a day, and a broken bookmark is flagged in the health view. Cheap, and enough for most bookmarks.
config.checkModeExplainMonitor: Answers a bigger question: how reliable has it been? It is checked on the interval you pick (from 5 minutes) and keeps history, so you get an uptime percentage, a heartbeat bar, outage history and optional alerts. Use it for the handful of services you actually care about being up.
config.checkModeExplainWhich: Monitor includes everything Periodic does, so there is never a reason to want both. Periodic suits your ordinary links; Monitor suits your own servers and dashboards. Monitoring everything would make a lot of network requests and a large history file for little benefit.
config.monitorNotifyDashboardUrlLabel: Address of this dashboard (for notification buttons)
config.pushNotifyNote: Sends notifications to this browser, even when nextDash is closed. Needs permission per device. Chrome also works on localhost; Safari requires HTTPS.
config.pushNotifyInfoMessage: Delivers alerts through your browser's push service, so they arrive even when nextDash is closed. Each device must allow notifications once. Requires HTTPS, or localhost during development; on iOS the app must be added to the home screen first.
config.pushNotifyEnabledOnDevice: Notifications are on for this device.
config.pushNotifyDisabledOnDevice: Notifications are off for this device.
config.pushNotifyBlocked: Notifications are blocked for this site. Allow them in your browser settings.
config.pushNotifyUnsupported: This browser does not support push notifications.
config.pushNotifyInsecure: Push notifications require HTTPS. Safari does not allow them on http://localhost — use an HTTPS address.
config.pushNotifyWelcomeFailed: Registered, but the first notification could not be delivered.
config.pushNotifyAskAgainDone: The invitation will appear again on the dashboard.
config.tagSuggestionsEmpty: Nothing to propose yet. Give three bookmarks from the same site the same tag and the rest of that site is offered it — or write a rule below and it proposes at once.
config.tagSuggestionsCapped: Showing the {shown} biggest suggestions of {total}. Accept some and the rest move up.
config.tagSuggestionNoneTicked: Nothing is ticked in that group, so there is nothing to apply.
config.removeBookmarkMessage: Are you sure you want to remove this bookmark? This action cannot be undone.
config.moveBookmarkMessage: Select the page to move this bookmark to:
config.createAndAddAnotherTitle: Save this bookmark and keep the form open to add another
config.removeCustomThemeMessage: Are you sure you want to remove this custom theme? This action cannot be undone.
config.hyprModeInfoMessage: HyprMode is designed for when nextDash is installed as a Progressive Web App (PWA). When enabled, clicking on bookmarks will open them in a new browser tab and then automatically close the PWA window, mimicking the behavior of a traditional app launcher.
config.lockLayoutInfoMessage: Turns off drag-and-drop reordering for bookmarks and categories, so the layout can't be moved by accident. Sorting, adding, renaming, and deleting still work as usual.
config.resetOnboardingHint: Show the quick-start card again on the dashboard (language, layout, weather, then the checklist), and bring back the one-time tours in Health and the inbox along with the occasional keyboard tips. Saves immediately.
config.sessionTipsHint: Now and then shows one keyboard tip as a toast on the dashboard — at most one every few days, never the same tip twice, and never during first-run setup.
config.tourReplayHint: Show one guided tour again. It appears where it belongs — in Health, the inbox, or wherever it explains.
config.tourReplayBlocked: Occasional keyboard tips are switched off, so no tour will appear until you turn them back on above.
config.tourNotSeenYet: You have not seen this one yet — it will appear on its own.
config.tourReplayError: Could not bring that tour back.

config.tourWhereHealth: the next time you open Health
config.tourWhereInbox: the next time you open the inbox
config.tourWhereFresh: the next time you open Fresh
