config.helpIntro: How nextDash works, where each setting lives, and which habits save time once the first week is behind you.
config.helpFirstHourBody:
nextDash works without any setup. These four steps turn an empty dashboard into one worth opening every morning.

Bring your bookmarks in. Config → Data & backups → Import browser bookmarks… reads the file every browser exports. Folders become categories, so the shape you already had survives the move.

Split them across pages. One page per context — work, home, a project — keeps each screen short. 1–9 jump between them.

Give the ten you open daily a shortcut. One or two letters, typed on the dashboard, open that bookmark. This is the change that makes the keyboard worth it.

Turn on link checking under Config → Behavior → Status & alerts if you want to know when a link dies. It runs in the background and reports in the health view.

Themes, layout and the header can wait until you have used nextDash for a week and know what you want.
config.helpStartDailyBody:
What the keyboard-first idea looks like once it is a habit:

  • Opening something you know. Type its shortcut. Or type part of its name and press Enter.
  • Keeping a link for later. Paste it on the dashboard. nextDash offers to add it as a bookmark or to put it in the inbox.
  • Looking something up. ? sends your text to a search engine or any site you defined as a finder.
  • Tidying as you go. Shift + E edits the selected bookmark, Shift + M moves it, Shift + T tags it. Deleted items stay in the trash for 30 days.
  • Once a month. The health view lists dead links, duplicates and bookmarks you have not opened in a long time.

If you forget a key, ! opens the cheat sheet over whatever you are doing.
config.helpStatsBody:
Config → Statistics counts what you have and what you use. It reads the data already on your server, so there is nothing to switch on. Five tabs:

  • Overview — the headline counts, and what the figures say, each with a button that acts on it
  • Activity — what you open: most-used bookmarks, which shortcuts earn their keys, which finders you use
  • Content — how bookmarks spread across pages and categories, what is untagged, and what is not a bookmark: widgets, feeds, sources, trash and backups
  • Inbox — how much is waiting, and how quickly links get handled
  • Health — the healthy share over time, uptime pooled across every monitor, certificates close to expiry, and how much of the collection has a local copy

Showing narrows every figure to one page. The inbox and the health report cannot be narrowed, and say so.

At the foot of every tab: when the figures were worked out, Refresh, and Export as CSV for all tabs at once. Visit Inbox and Health first if you want their figures in the file.
config.helpStatsReadingBody:
Some figures answer a sharper question than their label suggests:

  • Concentration — how much of your opening lands on how few bookmarks. A high number usually means the shortcuts work.
  • Opens per bookmark, by category — categories nobody opens from, often a name that no longer fits.
  • Cleanup candidates — never opened, opened once, untagged, still on http, without an icon. Show opens Config → Bookmarks with that filter applied.
  • Stale — not opened in a long time. Worth reviewing, not deleting on sight: a tax form you open once a year is stale and still wanted.

Where a period selector is offered, it changes the window the figures cover. A tag in Most used tags opens the bookmark list filtered to it.
config.helpStatsUsageBody:
Opening a bookmark from nextDash — by click, shortcut, search, the recent panel or the health view — adds one to its count and records the time. Activity, Concentration and Stale are built on that.

Two consequences:

  • Opening the same site from the browser's address bar does not count, so a site can look unused while you visit it daily.
  • A freshly imported collection starts at zero. Activity needs a few weeks of use; Overview and Content are right straight away.

The counts live in your own data files and travel with a backup. The side panel in Config → Bookmarks shows them per bookmark.
config.helpStatsPrivacyBody:
Everything under Statistics is worked out on your own server from your own data. None of it is sent anywhere.

Separately, nextDash can send anonymous product analytics that help decide what to build next. It is off unless you turn it on, has nothing to do with this page, and never includes bookmark names, URLs, tags or search text. The switch and a plain list of what is recorded are under Config → Behavior → Privacy & sync.
config.helpThemesBody:
Choosing a theme. nextDash ships 121 theme families, each with a light and a dark half. Browse… under Appearance → Look — or Shift + A from the dashboard — opens the theme browser: one card per family, a search box, filters for all, favourites, light and dark, and a star per family for the ones you use. Moving through it previews each theme on the real dashboard. Nothing is saved until you pick one, and Esc puts back what you had.

  • Quick mode switches between the light and dark half of the family you chose.
  • Follow system dark mode shows the light half by day and the dark half by night, following your operating system — also while the tab is in the background.
  • Random theme picks a new built-in theme on every page refresh, or on every view or page change. Your saved theme stays underneath and returns when you turn it off.

Surfaces. These settings change how any theme is drawn:

  • Depth — Flat (the default), Soft, Rich or Glass. The higher steps add a tint in the greys, raised surfaces and a wash of light behind the page. Glass blurs what is behind a surface.
  • Glow — how far the theme's colour carries around a surface: Off (the default), Soft or Full. Flat has no glow.
  • Text contrast — how far the fainter text sits from its surface, from Soft to Maximum.
  • Backdrop — the theme's own backdrop on or off, and a texture: follow the theme, dots, grid, lines, hatch or none. A background image of your own is drawn over it.
  • Favicon harmonization — pulls site icons toward the theme: Muted, Tinted or Overlay, with an intensity. It is stored per theme, so the light and dark halves are set separately.

Gloss themes. Ten families catch the light: Gloss Obsidian, Chrome, Candy, Amber, Emerald, Sapphire, Neon Tide, Pearl, Rose Gold and Ultraviolet, each light and dark. Their surfaces carry a lit band and a brighter top edge, with saturated accents, glass and a glow — lacquer rather than paint. They sort together in the theme browser; search for gloss. The shine needs the glow, so picking a Gloss theme while Glow is off offers to switch it on. Any other theme can get the same sheen: the Gloss slider in the theme editor sets it.

Type and background. Seven typefaces (three monospaced, four proportional), three weights and seven sizes — or upload a font file. The background follows the theme (Auto), is off, uses a gradient, or loads an image; opacity fades it so the bookmarks stay readable.

Custom themes. Appearance → Look → Make your own theme builds your own palette, with a contrast check that warns when text is too faint to read. A custom theme can set everything a packaged theme can — surfaces, glow, gloss, corner radius — and comes as a pair, so it has a light and a dark half like the built-in ones. Packaged themes on the same tab recolours a theme that ships; Reset defaults puts it back. A theme exports to a small JSON file (⤓ on its row) and imports on another install.
config.helpHeaderBody:
The header has three zones: the clock and weather with the page name on the left, the page switcher in the middle, and the destinations and action buttons on the right. Config → Appearance → Header sets the left and the middle and the destinations; Action bar sets the action buttons.

The destinations. Dashboard, inbox, health and config. Each can be switched off; its key keeps working. Button style draws them plain (underlined when current) or each in its own box.

The page switcher. Four styles:

  • Numbers beside the destinations — the default
  • One segmented control
  • Plain text, underlined — page names as tabs
  • One button with a list — for many pages or a narrow window

Page tabs shown before “+N” (3 to 9, four by default) sets how many pages show before the rest fold into a +N list. Every page keeps its digit key. Show page names in tabs and Show the dashboard title sit in the same group.

The action buttons. Add, search, commands, finders, tag cloud, recent, pages, fold-all and cheat sheet. Every button is on to begin with. Hiding a button leaves its key working; with every button off the surround goes too. Tags, recents, the cheat sheet and the pages panel open from the search panel as well, so a hidden button costs nothing.

Where the fixed buttons stand:

  • In a column on the right — the default — or on the left. The page moves aside to make room.
  • In a dock at the bottom — centred under the grid.
  • In the header — beside the destinations. Action buttons shown before “+N” (two by default) folds the rest behind one control, whose menu names each button with its key.
  • Behind one menu in the header — one control, every action in its menu.

A bar that slides away. Slide a docked bar away after takes 2 seconds (the default), 5, 10, 30, or always in view, and applies to the three docked positions. The bar comes back when the pointer touches that edge, when focus moves into it, and on ' or Shift + O, which also send it away. While it is away a small handle stands on that edge, growing and brightening as the pointer nears; a click on it brings the bar back. No handle in the header, behind the menu, or on a touch screen.

Show the key on each button puts the key chip on the buttons: on for a new install, off on a dashboard that already existed. With the chips off, resting on a button shows that button's key beside it. As the window narrows, the header folds its parts away in a fixed order, so the page switcher and the destinations stay reachable.

Commands change most of this without opening config: :switcher, :buttonstyle, :maxtabs, :maxactions, :buttons and :header.
config.helpNotificationsBody:
When a monitored bookmark goes down, nextDash can tell you — and again when it comes back, with how long it was down.

Downtime alerts (Behavior → Status & alerts) post to a service of your choice. Pick Slack, Discord, Telegram (bot URL and chat ID), Gotify, ntfy, Pushover (application token and user key) or Raw JSON for a receiver of your own. Only the fields the service needs are shown. An ntfy alert carries Open link and Health buttons; fill in Address of this dashboard for the second one.

Send test alert sends one made-up failure the same way a real one goes, so a wrong chat ID shows up now rather than during an outage.

Alert after sets how many failures in a row count as down (three by default), so one blip stays quiet.

Browser notifications reach your desktop or phone even with no dashboard open. Switch them on in the same place, press Enable on this device, and allow notifications once per browser. Downtime is on by default; backup results and new releases can be added. They need HTTPS — Safari and every browser on iPhone and iPad refuse them on plain http://localhost. On iPhone and iPad, add nextDash to the home screen first.

Silencing one bookmark. In a row's Expected response panel, tick Do not alert me about this bookmark. It is still checked and still shows as down, with a Muted badge; only the message is held back. Un-muting during an outage still alerts. In the health view, Mute alerts and Unmute change several rows at once.

When many fail at once — a host or proxy going down — the alerts are collapsed into one message that names the first few and counts the rest, rather than a burst that Slack or Telegram would rate-limit. Certificate warnings are always sent separately.
config.helpServerLogBody:
Config → Logs → Server logs shows what the server has been doing — background jobs, imports, checks and every request — without shell access to the machine.

Off by default. Switch on Record server log in the toolbar to start. While it is off nothing is captured and it costs nothing. Turning it off keeps what was collected.

Every line names its level and the part of the server it came from — WARN archive dash.example could not be saved: the page is behind a login — written for whoever runs nextDash.

  • Detail level decides what is written at all, here and in docker logs: Quiet (problems), Normal (what the server did) or Verbose (every step). It applies to the next line, without a restart.
  • Show only narrows what you look at: everything, warnings and errors, errors, or activity only. A note under it says which level is recording.
  • Search covers the whole log, not only what is on screen. Follow keeps the newest line in view.
  • Keep the log by age (an hour to 30 days, or until cleared) or by number of lines — one or the other.
  • Refresh polls every few seconds while the tab is open.

Copy and Download take the lines with you. Clear empties the log on screen and on disk. Anyone who can open config can read this log, including full webhook addresses where they were logged.
config.helpActivityTrailBody:
Logs → Activity trail chooses what goes into the machine-readable record: one JSON line per event, kept apart from the readable log. It is written to activity.log when NEXTDASH_ACTIVITY_LOG_PERSIST is set, and to the server log buffer.

Channels, in three groups:

  • Changes — what the server wrote or did: changes, check results, refused access, health rounds, imports, feed polls, saved copies, backups, failed writes, widget requests and alerts sent
  • Usage — what the person at the dashboard did: bookmarks opened, searches, keyboard shortcuts, navigation and dashboard loads
  • Client — errors the browser reported

Changes and check results are on by default; everything else is off until you tick it. Reset panel puts the defaults back.

Open detail sets how much a bookmark opened record carries: just the open, how it was opened (the default), or also its place in the results and how long you waited.

Environment variables set the same things for the whole server — the channels, the format (text or JSON), whether URLs are logged in full, by host or not at all, sampling per channel, and how long rotated files are kept. A choice made in the app wins over them. The README lists every variable.

Searches and URLs can end up in the trail, so treat the log files as private on a shared machine.
config.helpStartBody:
nextDash is a keyboard-first bookmark dashboard. Bookmarks sit in categories, categories sit on pages, and almost everything can be reached without the mouse.

The basics:

  • Start typing on the dashboard — the letters go to the search line. Enter opens the top result.
  • > search · : commands · ? finders — three modes of one panel
  • + adds a bookmark; pasting a URL on the dashboard offers to add it too
  • ! opens the cheat sheet, which lists every key
  • Give a bookmark a one- or two-letter shortcut and typing it opens that bookmark

The header. On the left: the clock and weather, with the name of the page or view. On the right: the page numbers, and the destinations — dashboard, inbox, health and config. The action buttons (add, search and the others you switch on) stand in a dock at the bottom by default; Config → Appearance → Action bar moves them into a side column, into the header or behind one menu.

First visit. A quick-start card asks for your language, layout and weather. Skip it whenever you like — every setting it touches stays in config.

Config, health and the inbox are views inside the dashboard, not separate pages. Nothing reloads, and Escape always takes you back to your bookmarks.
config.helpConfigBody:
Config is a view inside the dashboard. Open it with Shift + S, < or the gear in the header, and leave with Escape.

Every change saves the moment you make it. There is no Save button. A short message confirms the save, and most changes show on the dashboard straight away.

The sections in the left rail:

  • Overview — the figures of your collection, what needs your attention, how you use it, how tidy it is and whether the links still answer
  • Appearance — look (theme, type, background and your own themes), grid, rows, header, action bar, date and weather
  • Bookmarks — every bookmark in one list, plus tags, tag suggestions, your tag rules, list settings and local copies
  • Structure — categories, pages, finders and collections
  • Behavior — how the dashboard acts: general, keyboard & search, inbox & Fresh, status & alerts, privacy & sync
  • Data & backups — backups and import, sources, webhooks, icons & previews, trash, reset
  • Widgets — the blocks on your pages that show something other than links
  • Statistics — what is in your collection and how you use it
  • Help — this guide
  • Logs — the server log and the activity trail
  • About — what nextDash is, and News & features

Appearance and Behavior open on their settings. A row of tabs splits each by subject, every setting of a tab is on it, and a short line under each says what it does. Each opens on the tab you used last. Beside Appearance a small preview of your dashboard follows every change and marks the part the open tab is about. The filter and Only changed name the other tabs where they find something; a click takes you there.

Every setting explains itself. The ℹ beside a setting says what it does. A ↺ appears beside anything you changed, and puts back the default. Only changed hides everything still on its default, and Reset panel puts a whole group back.

Finding a setting. Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + K searches every section, tab, setting and help topic. It also matches what a setting is set to — search 8099 or Monitor when you know the value but not the name.

Coming back. Config reopens on the section and tab you left, for five minutes. An address like #config/appearance opens a section directly and can be bookmarked. The browser's Back button leaves config, the way Escape does.

Settings that follow you, and settings that do not. Settings live on the server, so every browser shows the same dashboard. Under Behavior → Privacy & sync you can keep appearance and layout on this device instead — useful when a laptop and a wall display should look different. The few settings that stay shared carry an all devices mark.

Copy a page or a category. Duplicate on a page row copies its categories and asks whether the bookmarks come too. On a category row it copies the category with its width, icon and sort. Copies start without check history, and copied bookmarks come without the original's shortcut.
config.helpAppearanceBody:
Config → Appearance opens on the tab you used last. A small preview of your dashboard stands beside the settings: it follows every change and marks the part the open tab is about. Six tabs:

  • Look — theme, light or dark, random theme, depth, glow, text contrast, backdrop, favicon styling, type, background and animations. Make your own theme… opens the editor for a palette of your own; ← Look brings you back.
  • Grid — columns per row, layout preset, density, category spacing, page margins, packed columns, hiding empty categories, launcher icon size, and how many bookmarks a category shows before show more. Categories across columns holds the settings for spread categories.
  • Rows — what a bookmark row shows: icons, the shortcut letters (always, only on the row you are on, or never), how far a row lights up when you move to it, status and ping, tags on the row, and link preview cards.
  • Header — the page switcher, the destinations and their button style, the title, where the clock and weather stand, and what the browser tab says: page name, custom title and favicon.
  • Action bar — where the action buttons stand, which of them show, and whether a docked bar slides away.
  • Date & weather — the clock and date format (12- or 24-hour) and the weather: your location or a city, Celsius or Fahrenheit, and how often it refreshes. The Weather widget reads the same settings. Two calendar addresses live here too: Calendar URL, which the date popover links to, and Calendar feed URL (.ics), which the Calendar widget reads.

Density is one setting for the whole app: the dashboard, health and the inbox all follow it. Auto adapts to the screen size and zoom.

Link preview cards. Hovering a bookmark opens a card: what the page is, what it says, and what you know about it — last check, uptime, certificate expiry, Fresh count, opens, shortcut and location. A row with nothing to say is left out. Rows → Link preview cards offers Off, On hover (the default) and Keyboard only; Shift + V opens the card for the selected row in every mode. A checklist decides which rows the card shows. The picture on the card is fetched by your server, not by your browser, so hovering tells the site nothing. Untick Image and no picture is fetched or stored. Data & backups → Icons & previews caps how much room the stored pictures take.

Finding a setting. Each tab has a filter beside Only changed; when it matches on another tab too, that tab is named under the list. Pointing at a type size or a theme previews it on the dashboard behind config; moving away puts it back.
config.helpBehaviorBody:
Behavior decides how the dashboard acts. It opens on the tab you used last. Five tabs:

  • General — language, whether a page remembers where you were scrolled, Lock layout, which stops drag-and-drop on bookmarks and categories, how links open, and Hypr mode for an installed app.
  • Keyboard & search — what typing a bookmark shortcut does, whether letters find names or shortcuts, fuzzy suggestions, finders among the results and how the search panel behaves; and the keys: those that work everywhere, the hints on header links, and the key legend under the grid.
  • Inbox & Fresh — whether the inbox exists, what pasting a URL on the dashboard does, and whether a bookmark shows how much its site published since you last opened it.
  • Status & alerts — link checking in this browser and on the server, how monitored bookmarks stand out, downtime alerts, maintenance windows and browser notifications.
  • Privacy & sync — the analytics opt-in, the daily check for a new release, posts from nextdash.cc, Keep settings on this device only, and the onboarding switches (tips, tours, review cards, the quick-start card again).

Most of these have a command as well, which is often quicker than opening config — see Search & keyboard → Commands.
config.helpWorkspaceBody:
Pages. Structure → Pages creates, renames, recolours, reorders and removes pages. Drag a row or use ↑ and ↓; the order is the order in the header. Page names must be unique. On the dashboard, double-click a page tab to rename it and give it an emoji and a colour dot.

The pages panel (,) lists every page with its bookmark count. New page (or n) creates one and takes you there; the × on a row deletes a page after asking twice. A deleted page goes to the trash with its categories and bookmarks.

Categories. Structure → Categories works the same way for the categories on one page. Names must be unique within a page; the same name on two pages is fine. Both lists show how many bookmarks each entry holds.

On the dashboard:

  • The + in a category header, or Shift + N, adds a category to the page you are on.
  • Right-click a category header — or Shift + F10 on it — to rename, spread, add, set an icon or delete. Deleting says how many bookmarks lose their category; the bookmarks are kept.
  • Drag the // in a category title to reorder, or press Alt + ← / Alt + → on a focused header.
  • F2 or a long press on the header renames it.
  • The bookmark form's Page and Category lists start with New page… and New category…, so a bookmark can go somewhere that does not exist yet.

Bookmarks without a category collect in an Other group at the end of the page.

Spreading a category across columns. Right-click its header and pick Spread across columns, or press Shift + W on it. Its bookmarks then flow across several columns. How many columns it takes follows from the items-per-category limit and how many bookmarks it holds, so it grows and shrinks with the category. Spreading needs a limit on items per category and at least two columns. Appearance → Grid holds the related settings.

You come back where you were. Switching pages, or opening health, inbox or config and coming back, returns you to the scroll position you left. Switch it off under Behavior → General.

Lock layout (Behavior → General, or :locklayout) stops dragging bookmarks and categories. Sorting, adding and editing still work.
config.helpBookmarksBody:
Config → Bookmarks has six tabs: List, Tags, Tag suggestions, Your rules, Settings and Local copies.

The list is a workbench in three parts.

  • The rail on the left narrows the list: a search (/), views such as Never opened or Without tags, and pages, categories, tags and health state, each with a count.
  • The list in the middle shows what is left, grouped and sorted as you choose. j/k or the arrows move, x ticks a row.
  • The side panel on the right shows the bookmark in focus and edits it in place: name, URL, page, category, tags, shortcut, note, pin, availability checking and interval. A list or a checkbox saves on change; a text field saves when you leave it; Escape puts the old value back. It also shows the bookmark's health and usage, and offers Show on dashboard, Refresh favicon and Delete.

Several at once. Tick rows and the side panel edits the whole selection: page, category, tags (add, replace or remove), pins and checking. A field that differs across the selection reads mixed. Apply writes the changes; Export CSV, Refresh favicons and Delete act on the selection. Bulk changes offer an undo in the toast.

Edit in dialog (Shift + E) opens the full bookmark form instead. Add bookmark opens the same form empty. The side panel folds away with Hide details; on a narrow screen the rail becomes a drawer and the panel a sheet.

What you narrowed the list to is kept in the address, so a filtered list is a link. A selection survives a filter change.

On the dashboard bookmarks work like a small spreadsheet. The arrows move the cursor, Shift + E edits the row in place, a long press does the same on touch. A click opens the bookmark; a drag reorders it or moves it to another category. Right-click a bookmark for all its actions — right-click inside a selection and the menu acts on the whole selection.

Pinned bookmarks stay at the top of their category. The rest follow the category's sort — manual, A–Z or Recent — set with the chips in its header. A sorted category cannot be dragged, and says so.

Adding. + opens the full form, & adds one in a single line (name | url | shortcut), pasting a URL offers to add it, and the browser extension saves the current tab.

A link you already have. The same URL twice on one page is refused. On another page, nextDash asks: “You already saved this on Work · Docs”, with a link to it. Save anyway keeps the second copy.

Settings holds what a new bookmark starts with, how the list opens, when a bulk action asks first, how many days count as stale, and which archive See an old copy uses.

Tag suggestions proposes a tag for whole groups of bookmarks at once. It works from your own rules, from the tags you gave a site's other bookmarks, and from a shipped list of 463 subjects. Each row names its source and count; the count opens the group so you can leave a bookmark out. Apply tags the rest with an undo; No thanks stops that proposal coming back. Read their pages is optional: it fetches the pages nothing else can place and files them by what they are about, after saying what it will cost. Your rules is where you write your own — github.com → #code — and they win over everything else.
config.helpTagsBody:
Tags are free labels on a bookmark. They are stored in lower case, trimmed and without duplicates, and autocomplete offers the ones you already use. Bookmarks → Tags renames or deletes a tag on every bookmark at once; renaming onto an existing tag is refused, so two tags are never merged by accident.

In search, tag:work narrows the results. The tag cloud (/) sizes each tag by use; click several and the dashboard shows bookmarks carrying any of them. Tags can also show on the rows themselves (Appearance → Rows); click one to filter.

Smart collections fill themselves — no rules to maintain. Turn them on under Structure → Collections:

  • Today — what you tend to open at this time of day, tuned by keywords for office hours, evenings and weekends
  • Recently opened and Recently added
  • Most used — ranked by opens, so it appears once you have opened bookmarks from the dashboard
  • Stale — not opened in a long time
  • Fresh — bookmarks whose site published something since you last opened them

Each has its own item limit and can be pointed at specific pages. They sit among your categories and fold the same way; editing a bookmark there edits the real bookmark.

Custom collections take rules of your own — tag, category or shortcut, matched with AND or OR, including excludes. Tag collections turn a tag into its own group once enough bookmarks carry it.
config.helpSearchBody:
Search, commands and finders are three modes of one panel: > search, : commands, ? finders. Type the prefix or click the mode at the top. What you typed stays when you switch.

Just type. On the dashboard the search line is always listening: letters go there and narrow the list. Enter opens the top result, ↑/↓ pick another, Ctrl/Cmd + Enter opens it in a new tab. Results are ranked by how well they match and how often you open them.

Typing a bookmark shortcut. By default a bookmark opens the moment what you typed matches its shortcut. If that swallows ordinary words of yours, Behavior → Keyboard & search → Typing a bookmark shortcut offers two alternatives: open after a short pause, which waits until you stop typing, and press Enter to open, where typing only narrows the list. The shortcut field in the bookmark form says which letters a shortcut costs you.

Names or shortcuts. Switch search mode (Behavior → Keyboard & search, or Shift + Q) decides whether bare letters look for a shortcut or a name. When one finds nothing and the other would, the panel offers a row that runs the search the other way.

While the cursor is on the grid the letters belong to the grid: j/k move, x ticks, g starts a jump, and a bookmark's own shortcut opens it. Esc drops the cursor and gives the letters back to search. Esc on a bare grid goes to your first page, and on the first page opens search.

Filters narrow results without changing the dashboard, and combine with each other and with plain words:

  • tag:work, category:news, page:2 (also page:current and page:all)
  • status: — online, offline, broken, ok, checked, unchecked, pinned, unpinned, tagged, untagged, noted, unnoted, feed
  • opened: and added: — today, week, month, year; opened:never finds what you never went back to
  • A leading - excludes: tag:dev -status:pinned is dev links I have not pinned

Search also matches your notes and the description nextDash fetched from the page.

Every page at once. Start the query with @ to search all pages. Shift + F is the opposite: it filters the page you are on in place, keeping the layout and the cursor.

From the browser's address bar. After one visit your browser knows nextDash as a search engine. Give it a short keyword in the browser's settings, then type the keyword, Tab, a term and Enter. A search also has its own address: #search?q=….

Behavior → Keyboard & search also holds fuzzy suggestions for near-misses, include finders in search, and keep search open when empty.
config.helpKeyboardBody:
Almost everything has a key. Panels: > search, : commands, ? finders, + add, & one-line add, ! or F1 the cheat sheet, / the tag cloud, * recent bookmarks, , the pages panel, Shift + A the theme browser. . folds or unfolds every category, Shift + N adds a category, ' slides a docked action bar away.

Views. Shift + H health, Shift + I inbox, Shift + S or < config. Escape backs out of any panel or view, and the browser's Back button returns to the view you came from.

Moving around the grid:

  • The first arrow key, Tab or a click starts the cursor
  • ↑ ↓ ← → move — k and j as well, once a row is selected; Enter or Space opens
  • 1–9 jump to a page · Shift + ← / Shift + → step between pages
  • G then a digit jumps to that category · G P to the first pinned bookmark
  • Home / End, Ctrl + Home / End and Page Up / Page Down jump further
  • Shift + Home steps up to the category header, where F2 renames, Shift + W spreads, Alt + ← / → moves, Delete deletes and Shift + F10 opens the menu
  • Esc clears the cursor; with nothing selected it goes to your first page

With a bookmark selected every action is Shift plus a letter, and the right-click menu shows each key:

  • Shift + E edit · Shift + V preview card · Shift + M move · Shift + T tags
  • Shift + D delete · Shift + P pin · Shift + C availability checking
  • Shift + L share or copy · Shift + R show the row in health · Ctrl + C copy the URL
  • Alt + ↑ / ↓ move it within its category · Shift + Alt + ← / → move it to the next category · t filter by its tag

Several at once. x ticks the selected bookmark and moves on, so a run is x x x; X takes its whole category. Shift + ↑ / ↓ extend the selection, Ctrl/Cmd + A takes everything on screen, and Alt-click or Shift-click do the same with the mouse. A toolbar offers move, tags, pin, checking, open, copy links and delete. The tag picker shows which tags the whole selection has, and which only some. Escape clears the selection.

The cheat sheet (!) lists every key, with a filter, and opens on the section for the view you are in. A printable PDF of all keys is linked at the top of this page.
config.helpConfigKeyboardBody:
Config has its own keys; the grid's keys do not run while it is open. ! lists them under Config view.

  • Sections. j/k step through the sections, g/G jump to the first and last. With the section rail focused, the arrow keys and Home/End work too.
  • Tabs. Alt + ← / → or [ / ] move between the tabs of any section.
  • Lists. In the Structure lists and Bookmarks → Tags, ↑/↓ move and Enter edits. In Bookmarks → List, j/k move, x ticks, Shift + E opens the edit dialog, m opens a row's menu and / focuses the search.
  • Controls. ←/→ move through a choice row and Space picks; Home/End set a slider to its minimum or maximum.
  • Finding. Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + K finds any section, tab, setting or help topic.
  • Leaving. 0–9 go to the inbox or a page. Escape closes an open dialog first, then clears a selection, then leaves config. Shift + S or < toggles config and reopens where you were.

Keys do not fire while you type in a field, except where a list says so.
config.helpHealthBody:
Every bookmark has an availability mode. Set it in the bookmark form, in the side panel under Config → Bookmarks, from the right-click menu, or with Shift + C:

  • Off — never checked
  • Periodic — checked now and then, and flagged when broken
  • Monitor — checked by the server on its own interval, from 5 minutes to 24 hours, with uptime history and alerts. Monitor includes everything Periodic does.

Once 20 or more bookmarks have no checking at all, a card in the bottom-left corner offers to switch them all to Periodic in one go. It names the count, shows at most once a month, and asks again if you say no — a second no offers to stop asking.

The check interval. On a monitored row the availability menu shows 5m, 15m, 30m, 1h, 6h and 24h. The interval also sets the time span of that row's heartbeat bar.

Behavior → Status & alerts holds the settings behind this: how often checks run in the browser and on the server, the check timeout (5 to 30 seconds), how many failures in a row count as down, spotting pages that answer 200 but say not found, the certificate warning window, and how much monitored bookmarks stand out on the dashboard.

A failure records why — DNS, timeout, refused, TLS, content or an HTTP status — so an outage names its cause. A failed check is tried again five seconds later and only counts if that fails too. A site that asks are you a robot reads as unknown, not as broken.

Services behind a sign-in. A self-hosted service answers not signed in to an anonymous check. In the health view, choose Expected response on the row: Sign in with picks a stored sign-in, Address to check instead points the check at a status endpoint while the bookmark keeps its own address, and a certificate this machine does not trust can be accepted. Sign-ins are stored from a Custom widget's settings and kept outside your backups. A sign-in is not sent along when a check is redirected to another host.
config.helpHealthViewBody:
The health view (Shift + H, or the pulse icon in the header) collects what needs attention across all pages. The icon carries a count: red for a broken link or a monitor that is down, amber for warnings.

The left column. At the top: the score, the trend with its sparkline, the broken count, uptime over 24 hours and the age of the report. Below: every filter with its count — broken, content, drift, duplicates, shortcut conflicts, stale, unchecked, unused, missing preview, certificates, healthy, monitored, ignored and all. A filter with nothing in it hides until it fills. Stale means not opened in over 30 days; Unused means never opened. A bookmark can match several filters at once. A sentence under the toolbar says what the active filter selects.

All monitors, under Sections, swaps the list for the panel about all monitors together — see Monitoring. It has its own address, #health/monitors.

The header stays put as you scroll: Work through, Rot report, the ⋯ menu (with Healthy over time and the exports), the ℹ explainer, and the density buttons. The report is built on the server, so the header says how old it is; Retest all rebuilds it.

Each row has a score from 0 to 100. Click the badge or press s to see what it costs: every bookmark starts at 100, and a broken link, a duplicate, a shortcut conflict, no check or no preview each take points off. Not opening a bookmark costs nothing. A row says when you last opened it and how long it has been failing. Group by site turns ten failures on one host into one group.

Fixing. The row menu (m, or a right-click) re-checks, follows a redirect, refreshes the title or icon, finds a copy in the Web Archive, saves a local copy, copies or shares the link, and deletes. Two duplicates can be merged into one, keeping both sets of tags and notes. n or z sets one condition aside for a bookmark you judged fine; the Ignored filter lists them. On the Missing preview filter, Fetch previews asks each page for its title, description and image.

Keys. j/k move, Enter opens, s score, p re-check, c checking mode, m more actions, i monitor statistics, f work through, R reload the report, g/G first and last, Esc back. A legend under the list shows them.

Several rows. Tick rows, or press x (X for everything the filter shows). The bar offers set checking, re-check, open, copy links, mute and unmute alerts, follow redirects, accept drift, rebuild previews, refresh favicons, save copies, and delete. The slow ones run one page at a time behind a progress bar. A row that changed since the report was built is skipped rather than deleted. Select all in the ⋯ menu ticks every row the filter shows, and reads Deselect all once they all are.

Work through (f) shows one row at a time with its actions large: re-check (p), open (Enter), delete (d), ignore for 30 days (z), skip (j) and back (k). It starts at the row your cursor is on, and stepping past either end says so rather than quietly wrapping round.

Ten links, two minutes. When enough links want attention, a card on the dashboard names what is waiting and Start runs a session over the worst ten. It ends with a count, offers another ten, and Done for today puts it away until tomorrow.

Rot report answers a different question: what has been happening to the collection — what has gone, what has moved or changed, what has failed for over a month, what is broken and was never opened, and what broke this week.
config.helpHealthStatsBody:
Monitored bookmarks keep a history for 30 days. Their rows show a heartbeat bar of recent checks, uptime over 24 hours with the number of checks behind it, and a response-time sparkline. The ⤢ button — or i on the row — opens the full picture: a response-time chart with minimum, average and maximum, uptime over 24 hours, 7 and 30 days, and the outages with start, length and cause. Point at the chart, or use ←/→, to read a single measurement. A window without samples reads no data, and a window the history cannot fill says how much it covers.

All monitors together. All monitors in the left column shows uptime pooled over every check in 24 hours, 7 and 30 days, how many monitors answer now, and the average response time. Below that: Least available (7 days), Slower than last week (the last day against the seven before) and Outages across the whole collection, newest first.

Health over time. Once the health view has been opened on two different days, Healthy over time in the ⋯ menu draws a chart. Buttons switch between healthy share, score, broken, monitors down, stale and unchecked. Percentages use a fixed 0–100 scale. One point is kept per day for 90 days; a day without a reading leaves a gap.

Exports. Export writes the filtered list as CSV, with interval, uptime, last response time and check count for monitored rows. Export history, on the Monitored filter, writes every single check: time, up or down, ping and HTTP status.
config.helpHealthExpectBody:
A plain check asks one question: did the host answer? A shop that answers Database connection failed answers fine, and passes.

On a monitored row, choose Expected response in the availability menu. The row opens a panel with two optional tests:

  • Text the page must contain — a phrase that only appears when the page works. Capitals do not matter. Fail if present instead reverses it, for an error banner or a parked-domain notice.
  • Status codes that count as healthy — by default anything below 500 counts, because 401 and 403 are normal behind a login. Name the codes yourself — 200, 200-299, 200,301,401 — when only some answers are right. A code nextDash cannot read is ignored, so a typo cannot take a working bookmark down.

These failures get their own Content filter, apart from Broken: a server that is down and a page that shows the wrong thing need different fixes. The row names the phrase or code it expected.

The same panel holds Watch for redirects, retitling and rewrites and Do not alert me about this bookmark. Clearing both test fields clears the failure they caused.

Pages that say not found with a 200. With Spot pages that answer 200 but say not found on (Behavior → Status & alerts), a monitored check reads the page title and opening text for a not-found message. A site that sends every address to a sign-in page is left alone.
config.helpHealthCertBody:
An expiring certificate is invisible to an ordinary check: the site works until the morning it does not.

Every check over HTTPS already completes a TLS handshake, so nextDash reads the expiry date from it. Nothing to switch on, no extra request.

A Certificates filter appears in the health view once one is close, and the affected rows carry a badge with the days left. Warnings go out at 30, 7 and 3 days through the same webhook and browser notifications as downtime. Behavior → Status & alerts sets when the warning starts.

Certificates belong to a host: ten bookmarks on one domain share one, and one renewal clears all ten. Renewing re-arms the warnings for the next expiry.
config.helpHealthDriftBody:
A bookmark can answer 200 OK while the page behind it is no longer the page you saved: a post replaced by a listing, a product page that redirects to the shop's front page, a lapsed domain with a for-sale notice. Drift watches for that.

Turn it on per bookmark. On a monitored row, choose Expected response and tick Watch for redirects, retitling and rewrites. The next check becomes the baseline: where the link landed, the page title, and a rough fingerprint of the text. Every later check is compared with that baseline, not with the previous check, so a slow change cannot slip past.

  • Redirect drift — the link now lands somewhere else. Another host is the strongest signal, the site's front page the next. http to https, www., a trailing slash and tracking parameters are ignored.
  • Title drift — the title changed. A title such as Domain for sale or 404 — Page not found is named outright; an ordinary retitle is flagged more gently.
  • Content drift — the text became a different page in substance, not just a new date in the footer.

One finding per check, in that order. The badge reads Moved, Retitled or Changed; hovering it gives the full sentence. The Drift filter collects them. A page that returns to its baseline clears itself.

Reading the page body costs bandwidth, so drift is opt-in and only for monitored bookmarks.

Accepting a change you expected. A rebrand or a move to a new domain trips drift on every bookmark for that site. Tick those rows and use Accept drift: it clears the finding and drops the baseline, so the next check records the page as it is now. Accepting says the new page is the right one — a page that really rotted would be marked healthy — so it only acts on rows you picked.
config.helpHealthMaintenanceBody:
A self-hosted service that goes down for ten minutes every night — a backup, a restart — is not broken. Without a maintenance window, each of those gaps is an incident, an alert and a dent in the uptime figure.

Under Config → Behavior → Status & alerts → Maintenance windows, add a window with days, a start and an end — Sunday 02:00–02:30 for a weekly job. An end earlier than the start runs past midnight. Windows apply to every monitor.

Inside a window checks still run and the heartbeat still records them. A failure there does not open an incident, does not count against uptime and sends no alert. An outage that is still going when the window closes raises the alarm as usual.
config.helpHealthWalkthroughTitle: Setting up one monitored bookmark, start to finish
config.helpHealthWalkthroughBody:
All of it on one bookmark, in the order you would set it up: a self-hosted status page at https://status.example.com, behind a login and backed up every night at 3am. The first time you open the health view, a tour walks the same example.

1. Turn on Monitor. Right-click the bookmark and set availability checking to Monitor. The server now checks it whether or not the dashboard is open.

2. Pick an interval. The availability menu now shows Check interval. A status page people rely on deserves 5 minutes.

3. Say what up means. Behind a login the page answers 401 to the check. Choose Expected response and type 200,401 in Status codes that count as healthy, so a real outage stands out. If the page shows All systems operational when all is well, put that in Text the page must contain.

4. Watch for the page changing. Tick Watch for redirects, retitling and rewrites. If the domain lapses or a proxy starts sending it elsewhere, drift catches what the rules above cannot.

5. Leave out the backup. Under Behavior → Status & alerts → Maintenance windows, add a daily window from 03:00 to 03:10. Without it, every nightly restart is an incident and an alert.

6. Wire up an alert. Under Downtime alerts, pick the service you already watch — Slack for a team, Pushover for a phone. Set Alert after to 3 failures, and press Send test alert to see it arrive.

From then on the row shows a heartbeat and an uptime figure, the Monitors panel counts it, and a real outage reaches you within minutes.
config.helpInboxBody:
The inbox (Shift + I, 0 or :inbox) holds links you want to keep before you know where they belong.

Getting links in. Paste a URL on the dashboard: depending on Behavior → Inbox & Fresh it becomes a bookmark, goes to the inbox, or you are asked. The browser extension has a Save to Inbox button, and the share sheet and bookmarklet (below) save here too. A URL already in the inbox is not added twice: a toast says Already in Inbox and you are taken to the existing row.

Read and unread. A new link is unread until you open it or keep it with r or Space. The inbox icon in the header counts the unread links, and pulses when one arrives until you first open the inbox. Read links stay until you clear them; right-click a read link to mark it unread again.

Each link can be opened, given a note (n), tagged, snoozed, promoted to a bookmark or deleted with undo. A note is plain text, not markdown. The page description fetched on capture shows under the title.

Promoting (p) opens the bookmark form filled in, with every page and category to choose from. The inbox entry goes once the bookmark is saved.

The ℹ at the end of the toolbar explains the inbox from inside the view.
config.helpInboxWorkBody:
Filters sit in a left column, each with its count: all, unread, snoozed and with note (the last two only when they hold something). This week above them is a readout. Narrow further by site, by tag or by search. Every count follows what the view shows, and Mark all read becomes Mark shown read while something narrows the list.

Sorting — newest first, oldest first, title or site. Oldest first is how a backlog gets cleared.

Snoozing (z) hides a link until three hours from now, tomorrow, the weekend, next week or a date you pick. A snoozed link is left out of every count until it wakes. Wake now brings it back early; a line under the list says how many are asleep.

Keys. j/k move, g/G jump to the first and last row, Enter opens, x ticks a row, R reloads, Escape clears the selection.

Several at once. Tick rows and the bar offers promote (to one page), open, copy links, mark read, snooze and delete. Select all in the ⋯ menu ticks every link the filters leave, and reads Deselect all once they all are.

Export and import. CSV and JSON export what the view shows. Import reads a JSON export back in, skipping links already there.

Filter, sort, site and search are kept in the address, so a view can be bookmarked. Filter, sort and site also return on your next visit. Rows follow the density set for the whole app, and the header stays in place as you scroll.
config.helpInboxTriageBody:
Triage shows one link at a time and works entirely from the keyboard. Start it with the Triage button, t in the list, or :inbox triage.

j/k move, o or Enter opens, p promotes, r or Space keeps it and marks it read, d or Delete removes it. Each action moves on to the next link. Escape returns to the list where you left off.

Triage follows the filter and sort you had. From Unread, oldest first, you work the backlog in the order you have been avoiding it.
config.helpInboxSettingsBody:
Config → Behavior → Inbox & Fresh has one switch that matters most: Enable the inbox. Turn it off and the inbox leaves the header, its keys and command stop working, and a pasted URL is added straight as a bookmark.

Two settings exist only in the settings file:

  • A cap on the number of links (inboxMaxItems, 500 by default). Past it, the oldest links are silently dropped — a reason to work the inbox down with triage.
  • Deduplicating by URL, on by default.

Both apply as soon as the file changes.

At the cap, undo still works. Undoing a delete puts the link back with its original date, and the oldest of the others makes way for it. If there is no room at all, the undo says the inbox is full.
config.helpInboxTourBody:
The first time you open the inbox, a short tour walks through it in seven steps: where links come from, what read means, snoozing, notes, promoting, triage and selecting several. It appears once; finishing, skipping and Escape all count as seen.

Behavior → Privacy & sync → Onboarding can play it again, and Show quick-start card again brings back every tour and hint. Turning off the keyboard tips there stops the one-time hints from appearing.
config.helpDataBody:
Config → Data & backups has six tabs: Backups & data, Sources, Webhooks, Icons & previews, Trash and Reset.

Backups. A backup is a ZIP of the whole data directory: bookmarks, pages, finders, the inbox, settings, themes and check history. What a backup carries decides whether local copies of pages and stored tokens go in too. Make a backup now stores one on the server; Download backup saves one to your computer.

Automatic backups run on a schedule — every day, week (the default), two weeks or month — and the newest three are kept. NEXTDASH_AUTO_BACKUP_KEEP raises that number and NEXTDASH_AUTO_BACKUP_DIR stores them elsewhere. Each stored backup shows its age, size and contents, with Download, Restore and Delete. The Last backup tile turns red when a scheduled run fails. In Docker, keep the data directory on a mounted volume so backups survive a rebuild.

Restoring replaces what is there. nextDash first writes a backup of the current data, so a restore can be undone. An archive without bookmarks in it is refused.

Import and export. Import browser bookmarks… reads the HTML file every browser exports — and that Pocket, Pinboard, Raindrop, linkding, Shiori, Linkwarden and Karakeep export too. Folders become categories; tags, notes and dates come along; duplicates are skipped. Export bookmarks (HTML) writes the same format. The CSV pair lets you tidy bookmarks in a spreadsheet and read them back, tags and notes included. :backup and :export reach this from the dashboard.

Icons & previews refreshes favicons, refreshes or clears the stored link previews, caps the image cache at 50, 200 or 500 MB, and forgets the keywords Read their pages collected.

Trash. Deleted bookmarks, pages and categories stay for 30 days — :trash opens it. A deleted page is one entry and comes back with its categories and bookmarks, in its old place. Search the trash, restore several at once, or delete for good. A restore that cannot go ahead — a category whose page is gone — is refused and the item stays.

Reset deletes all bookmarks, or everything. Both ask first; make a backup before you use them.

Your data is plain JSON in one directory, and open dashboard tabs refresh themselves when another tab saves.
config.helpSourcesBody:
An import reads a file once. A source keeps sending bookmarks and is asked again later. Sources have their own tab: Data & backups → Sources.

  • GitHub stars — needs a personal access token
  • Raindrop.io — needs a test token
  • Hacker News favorites — just your username
  • YouTube channel — just a handle or channel id; follows the channel's public feed
  • Mastodon bookmarks — needs an access token from your instance

Every source asks the same things: the token, where its bookmarks go, import now, and what happened last time. Each one previews what it would write before writing, and remembers where it got to, so a second run only brings what is new. nextDash only reads from these services. The Sources widget shows the last result of each source on your dashboard.

Tokens live in their own file, readable only by the account nextDash runs as, and stay out of backups unless you include stored tokens.
config.helpArchiveTitle: Keeping a copy of a page
config.helpArchiveBody:
The health view tells you a link is dead. A copy means you can still read it. Both kinds are set up under Data & backups → Sources.

The Web Archive. Switch on Archive new bookmarks and the Internet Archive is asked to keep a copy the day you save a link. Without an archive.org key pair the daily allowance is small, so the panel takes an access key and secret, and a button captures one page to test them. A capture is queued; the panel says what became of it.

A copy on your own disk. Local copies saves a whole page — text, styling and images — as one file in your data directory. It stays readable when the site and the archive are both gone. Bookmarks → Local copies lists them per bookmark, says when a copy failed or saved an empty page, and can remove them all at once. The health view saves copies for a whole selection.

archive.today is a second opinion: it keeps what it captured, where the Web Archive drops what a site withdraws.

Finding an old copy. A row's menu in the health view opens the archive's captures, or points the bookmark at the last good copy — the original address goes into the note. The archive used here is set under Bookmarks → Settings.
config.helpIntegrationsBody:
nextDash asks other services for things on its own schedule. Webhooks work the other way round: Data & backups → Webhooks tells another program the moment something happens here.

Give a receiver a name and an address and tick the events it should hear about: a bookmark added, changed or removed, and a monitored bookmark going down or coming back. Nothing ticked means everything.

Every delivery is signed with the Standard Webhooks scheme, so the receiver can check it came from this install. The signing key is shown once, when you save; copy it then.

A failed delivery is tried twice more and then dropped. A refusal from the receiver is not retried. Send a test posts one delivery and shows the answer. A local address only works when local bookmarks are allowed.
config.helpWidgetsBody:
A page holds categories of bookmarks, and it can also hold widgets: blocks that show something other than links. They stand among your categories, are dragged into place the same way, and share one order with them.

Most widgets read what nextDash already keeps — the health report, check history, the inbox, feeds, sources, the trash, backups and your own open counts. Nothing new is polled for them. A figure on a tile is a link: click the broken count and you land on those bookmarks. A few read further: Weather and Calendar, the system widgets, RSS, and the Custom widget.

One column or two. Two is the maximum. On a single-column dashboard a wide widget narrows itself.

A tile says what it left out. A widget with a row limit shows 5 of 12, not a silent five.

Folding. Click a widget's title, or press Enter on its header, and it folds shut like a category. . folds every block on the page, widgets included. Each block stays as you left it, per page.

From its own header. Right-click a widget's title to rename it, make it one or two columns wide, fold it, open its settings or close it. Closing hides the widget and keeps its settings; Config → Widgets switches it back on. The arrow keys walk into a widget and through its rows, and Enter does what clicking the row does.

Refreshing. A widget that reads something outside refreshes on its own interval while the tab is visible, and asks nothing while the tab is in the background. Right-click a Custom widget's title for Refresh now.
config.helpSelfHostingBody:
nextDash runs as one binary or container, stores everything as plain JSON in one data directory, and needs no database. Mount that directory as a volume and an upgrade is a new image. Backing up the directory backs up everything.

Production Docker. docker-compose.prod.yml mounts only ./data; the assets are built into the binary. The container runs as the user nextdash with a memory cap. docker-compose.proxy.yml with deploy/Caddyfile adds TLS in front. docker-compose.yml is for development.

Access. There are no accounts: anyone who can reach the address can read and change your data. Keep nextDash on your own network or behind a reverse proxy with authentication, and never expose plain HTTP to the internet. NEXTDASH_WRITE_TOKEN protects every write; the dashboard supplies it for you. The data directory is not served — only icons and an uploaded favicon or font are.

Privacy. There is no telemetry beyond the opt-in analytics under Behavior → Privacy & sync.

The browser extension saves the current tab to a page or to the inbox, with a shortcut, tags and a note. It needs your server address, and the write token if you set one.

If something looks wrong. Bookmarks that seem gone are usually hidden by a filter in the Bookmarks list. An unexpected order usually means a category sorted A–Z or Recent, or a pinned bookmark. Search that misses something often has a filter like tag: still in the box. The README and the manual on GitHub cover the compose files and every environment variable.
config.helpAboutBody:
nextDash is a self-hosted, keyboard-first bookmark dashboard: fast to search, quick to organise, and yours to host. No accounts, no tracking, no database — your bookmarks in plain files on a server you control.

Two tabs. This one is about the project. News & features carries every post from nextdash.cc, every release and every setting worth switching on, with filters per source. A button there saves nextdash.cc as a bookmark, so Fresh can count its posts.

nextdash.cc is the project's site. jordibrw.nl is where the person behind it writes. Issues, requests and release notes are on GitHub, and the Ko-fi link below is the way to say thanks.
config.helpVersionBody: The heading names the release this install runs. See what's new opens the release notes, newest first, with the earlier releases underneath. The complete history is in the changelog on GitHub.
